items.title: A-81 Reaches South Georgia
items.short_description: The Antarctic iceberg made a relatively quick exit from the Weddell Sea, only to slow at the edge of a remote island’s underwater shelf.
items.abstract: The Antarctic iceberg made a relatively quick exit from the Weddell Sea, only to slow at the edge of a remote island’s underwater shelf. Others, like Iceberg A-81, make a faster exit, heading north out of the Weddell Sea along a route well-traveled by the region’s bergs. In the days before, its progress slowed noticeably, and it appeared to be bumping along the edge of the island’s underwater shelf, according to Jan Lieser of Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology and Christopher Shuman of the University of Maryland (retired). Calving is a normal part of the life cycle of ice shelves, but scientists keep a close eye on Brunt, which has recently shed several large icebergs in quick succession and is home to the British Antarctic Survey’s Halley Research Station, a major base for Earth, atmospheric, and space science research since the 1950s.

items.title: Hunting Red Leaves with Satellites
items.short_description: A modern satellite makes it possible to pursue the ancient tradition of leaf-peeping in a whole new way.
items.abstract: A modern satellite makes it possible to pursue the ancient tradition of leaf-peeping in a whole new way. The Japanese tradition of momijigari, or "red leaf hunting," stretches back more than a millennium, as evidenced by ancient poems describing journeys to admire fall foliage. Tracking the ratio over time reveals where leaves are changing and when color peaks. Areas shown in green have values near 1, meaning the satellite detects about as much red as green, and most leaves have not yet turned. Huemmrich, who is also a member of the PACE science team, was eager to work with the satellite because of OCI's broad swath and short revisit time. The PACE team is asking the public to submit photos of fall foliage to help scientists "ground truth" the satellite observations and better understand how various factors influence vegetation color.

items.title: El Niño Then and Now
items.short_description: A 35-year satellite altimetry record lets scientists hold this year's El Niño up against its strongest predecessors.
items.abstract: A 35-year satellite altimetry record lets scientists hold this year's El Niño up against its strongest predecessors. Data are from the TOPEX/Poseidon satellite and the Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich satellite, respectively, and were processed by scientists at JPL. “What’s unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next,” Willis said. “That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. Sea surface height anomalies on October 12, 2015, based on altimetry data from the Jason-2 satellite, are shown above in context with maps from around the same time in 1997 and 2026. NASA Earth Observatory maps by Lauren Dauphin, using NASA-SSH altimetry data provided by Josh Willis, Severine Fournier, and Kevin Marlis, NASA/JPL-Caltech.

items.title: Fires Char New Guinea
items.short_description: Emissions on both sides of the island are unusually high as human-set fires spread in a landscape parched by drought.
items.abstract: Emissions on both sides of the island are unusually high as human-set fires spread in a landscape parched by drought. But in September and October 2026, as drought gripped New Guinea (sometimes called Papua) amid a strong El Niño, fires scorched the island and smoke shrouded large swaths of it for weeks. According to the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), a fire emissions monitoring system, fires in Papua New Guinea, on the eastern half of the island, had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon by October 17, more than any other year on record at that point in the year (charts above). In dry conditions, managed fires sometimes spread and burn uncontrolled as wildfires, particularly in the drier, southernmost parts of the island.

items.title: Extratropical Cyclone Whips Past Iceland
items.short_description: The powerful low-pressure system formed over the North Atlantic out of the remnants of Hurricane Isaias.
items.abstract: The powerful low-pressure system formed over the North Atlantic out of the remnants of Hurricane Isaias. Hurricane Isaias—the only Atlantic hurricane to date in 2026—made landfall in Florida as a Category 2 storm on October 9. Riding the jet stream east over the North Atlantic, Isaias’s remnants developed into a powerful storm known as an extratropical cyclone. The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-21 satellite captured this image of the extratropical cyclone brushing past Iceland on the afternoon of October 14. The cyclone lashed Iceland with high winds as it grazed the coast. Farther across the Atlantic, northwestern Scotland received gusts up to 90 kilometers (55 miles) per hour on October 14, according to news reports, resulting in cancellations on several ferry routes.

items.title: The Human Fingerprint on Earth’s Water Cycle
items.short_description: Human activities have become intertwined with how water is distributed across the continents. A new study brings their effects into sharper focus.
items.abstract: Human activities have become intertwined with how water is distributed across the continents. A new study brings their effects into sharper focus. Humans are exerting increasing influence over how water moves through lakes, rivers, soil, and the subsurface, and a new NASA study shows where those effects are greatest. Beyond the influence of climate variability, the scientists identified 40 regions where the changes also aligned with human activities such as irrigation, reservoir impoundment, and land-use change. In some areas, the effects of human activities were especially strong. In the new analysis, the Boguchany Reservoir on Russia’s Angara River, the second-largest reservoir filled in the 21st century, produced the strongest water storage trend in nonpolar northern Asia. Moving forward, O’Neill wants to capture how dams, diversions, irrigation, and other controls on Earth’s water affect storage downstream, and to disentangle the influence of local and non-local activities.

items.title: Autumn Paints Poland’s Bieszczady Mountains
items.short_description: Fall color covers the forested slopes of Bieszczady National Park, while patches of polonina, a type of high-mountain meadow, have turned tan.
items.abstract: Fall color covers the forested slopes of Bieszczady National Park, while patches of polonina, a type of high-mountain meadow, have turned tan. The seasonal transformation was underway in southeast Poland’s Bieszczady National Park on October 8, 2026, when the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite captured this image. Portions of Bieszczady National Park are included within UNESCO’s network of ancient and primeval beech forests spanning 18 countries. Above that is the realm of the polonina, a Slavic term for subalpine meadow, consisting of open grasslands and shrubby thickets of rowan (mountain ash), willows, and green alder. Patches of polonina stretch across ridge tops to the east-southeast of Smerek and appear tan, having lost their summer greenness.
